messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 68

# The Weight of the Kitchen

Maria is fifty-four years old, a head chef with nearly three decades of experience running professional kitchens. She has always been someone who thrives in controlled chaos — the heat, the noise, the relentless pace of service. Her husband describes her as the most capable person he has ever known. She describes herself, now, as someone she no longer recognizes.

Two years ago, Maria was closing down her restaurant late on a Tuesday night. The rest of the staff had gone home. She was alone in the back alley taking out the final bags of refuse when a man she had never seen before attacked her. He grabbed her from behind, slammed her against the brick wall, and beat her badly enough that she lost consciousness. She woke up on the cold ground, her face against the wet asphalt, unsure at first where she was or what had happened. Her handbag was gone. Her sense of safety never came back.

In the weeks that followed, Maria told herself she was fine. She returned to work within ten days, moving through her kitchen with deliberate efficiency, refusing to let her staff see her struggle. But something had shifted fundamentally in how she experienced the world. The alley behind the restaurant became impassable for her. She began parking three streets away and entering through the front, arriving before anyone else so she could check every corner of the building alone. She stopped staying late.

The nights became the worst of it. Maria lies awake for hours, her body rigid beside her sleeping husband, listening to sounds in the house that she cannot stop cataloguing as threats. When she does sleep, she returns to the alley — not as a dream exactly, but as something more total than that, a complete re-entry into the moment she felt hands close around her. She wakes gasping, drenched, her heart hammering so hard she has pressed her hand to her chest more than once to confirm it is still beating.

In the kitchen, the symptoms have found their own particular shape. A prep cook who comes up quickly behind her to reach for a pan will send her stumbling backward, her hands raised, a sound leaving her throat that she cannot control. She has snapped at staff members with a ferocity that frightens her afterward. She used to love the controlled violence of the kitchen — the cleavers, the fire, the urgency — but now the sounds of metal and shouting move through her like electricity, and she has to grip the edge of the pass to stay present in the room. The creativity that once defined her cooking has largely deserted her. She writes the same menus she has written for years because novelty requires a kind of openness she no longer has access to.

Maria's husband knows something is wrong, though she has told him only the bare outline of what happened and almost nothing of what continues to happen inside her. She has become, she says quietly, someone who flinches. She does not go out in the evenings. She avoids the neighborhood where the restaurant sits when she is not working. She canceled a trip to visit her sister in Portugal because the thought of being in an airport, surrounded by strangers, produced a panic so complete she spent an afternoon sitting on the kitchen floor at home, unable to explain to her husband why she could not get up.

What Maria returns to, again and again, is a particular thought that has lodged itself at the center of her life: that she did not see it coming, and that this means she will never be safe again. She had always trusted her instincts. She had always known her environment. The attack did not just hurt her body. It dismantled the story she had told herself about who she was — a woman in command of her surroundings, competent and alert and unafraid. She is still running her kitchen. She is still cooking. But she is doing it, she says, from somewhere very far away.
